prompts.car_park:
Write short messages for a test set. The messages are notes left by drivers at a car park, from which the driver's permit can be told.

Write 12 different messages for each of these labels:
- resident: the driver lives locally and holds a resident permit
- visitor: the driver is visiting and holds no permit
- staff: the driver works at the site and holds a staff permit

Each message is one to three sentences of natural English, as a real person would write it. Vary the wording, length and style. A careful reader must be able to tell which label a message belongs to, and it must not fit any other label.

Reply with JSON only, no code fence: an object with the keys "resident", "visitor", "staff", each mapping to an array of 12 strings.

water: All twelve bottles came back clear with no visible sediment; pH is holding at 7.2 across the batch.
Turbidity readings are under 1 NTU for every sample, so I went ahead and filtered the replicates.
The tap water controls look fine, but two of the field samples have a faint chlorine smell.
I labeled the aliquots and stored them at 4 °C; conductivity is around 540 µS/cm for most of them.
One bottle leaked in transit, so I only have 200 mL left for that one, but the rest are full.
These are all aqueous, so I ran them on the TOC analyzer first thing this morning.
The membrane filters came back clean after 48 hours, and the samples themselves stayed crystal clear.
I adjusted the pH of the Milli-Q blanks before spiking them with the standard.
The surface water samples have a slight green tint, probably algae, but the lab water is colorless.
I measured 250 mL into each graduated cylinder and recorded the temperature before testing.
All the rinse water was collected in the waste container; the samples themselves are in the fridge.
Salinity looks consistent with last week's batch, around 0.5 ppt for the estuary samples.
soil: The cores came in still damp, so I weighed them before and after oven-drying to get gravimetric moisture.
I sieved everything through a 2 mm mesh and removed the roots and stones before bagging the fines.
Texture feels like a sandy loam for most of these; a couple are heavier clay near the bottom of the plot.
I recorded the horizon for each sample, since the topsoil and subsoil look quite different in color.
The samples are still field-moist, so I put them in the drying oven at 105 °C overnight.
I homogenized each bag and split it into subsamples for the pH and organic matter tests.
There's a lot of grit in these; I had to rinse the auger between cores to avoid cross-contamination.
Bulk density rings were taken at two depths, and the soil was pretty compacted at the lower one.
I air-dried the samples on the bench, then ground them with the mortar and pestle for the nutrient panel.
The pH is around 6.5 for the agricultural plots, a bit lower than the forest samples.
I kept the samples in paper bags so they could breathe; the plastic liners were only for transport.
One core collapsed when I tried to section it, but I still got enough material for the archive.
blood: All the EDTA tubes were filled to the line and inverted gently eight times right after collection.
I centrifuged the samples at 3000 rpm for ten minutes and the plasma separated cleanly.
Two of the tubes show slight hemolysis, so I flagged them before loading the analyzer.
The whole blood samples were kept at room temperature and mixed on the roller for twenty minutes.
I aliquoted the serum into cryovials and froze them at -80 °C within the hour.
Clotting time was normal for most, but one sample didn't clot fully in the SST tube.
I labeled each vacutainer with the barcode and checked that none were underfilled.
The red cell count came back low on sample 7, so I made a smear to double-check morphology.
I thawed the plasma aliquots on ice and ran the coagulation panel straight away.
The buffy coat was visible in every tube after spinning, which is what we expected.
I disposed of the sharps and the used needles in the biohazard container after processing.
Hemoglobin levels are within range for the batch, and the samples were stored at 2–8 °C overnight.
